1 
 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
CITY OF SOMERVILLE, MASSACHUSETTS 
SCHOOL COMMITTEE 
 
     Monday, August 31, 2026 - Regular Meeting 
 
 
7:00 p.m. – City Hall Chambers  
 
Members present: Council Davis, Rep. Pitone(arrived at 7:04), Rep. Lippens, Rep. Eldridge, Rep. Green, Dr. 
Stellman, Mayor Wilson (arrived at 7:19), Rep. Biton, and Chair Ackman. Members Absent:  
 
I.  CALL TO ORDER 
The meeting was called to order at  7:01 pm with a moment of silence, followed by a salute to the flag of the United 
States of America. Chair Ackman asked Superintendent Carmona to call the roll, the results of which were as follows: 
PRESENT – 9 – President Davis, Member. Pitone, Member. Lippens, Member. Eldridge, Member Green, Dr. Stellman, 
Mayor Wilson, Member Biton, and Chair Ackman.  ABSENT  
 
VII - COMMUNITY OR CALENDAR ITEMS FROM BOARD MEMBERS (Out-of-Order) 
 
Chair Dr. Ackman: With the Committee’s consent, I will note that there is no public comment today. I will move to an 
item under New Business, Community or Calendar Updates from Committee Members, as I believe this discussion qualifies 
as a community update. 
At the end of the last school year, it was brought to my attention that, during public comment, there is currently no way 
for the Chair to shut off the microphone if an individual begins speaking in a manner that is unlawful or could potentially 
expose the District to legal action. 
As the Chair overseeing public comment, I reached out to the City regarding this concern. We initially discussed the 
possibility of using a buzzer; however, I want to clarify that we first consulted with legal counsel. Legal counsel expressed 
concern that, without a way for the Chair to shut off the microphone, the Committee and District could potentially be 
exposed to legal liability if someone were to make comments that are unlawful or could result in a lawsuit.  
We have reached out to the Cit y, and our new Chief Strategy and Operations Officer has done a great job working on 
this issue. We were informed that an alternate microphone setup is possible; however, the City is asking the District to 
cover the cost of the alternate setup. 
I think it is important to bring this matter to the Committee because implementing the alternate setup would require a 
reallocation of funds. Public comment is very important. Someone who reached out to me yesterday, and I will attempt 
to quote them, said that public comment is “a foundational aspect of our democracy.” I could not agree more.  
I did not make this decision lightly, but I also do not believe that leaving the Committee and District legally exposed is a 
responsible choice. I wanted to bring this matter forward as a community update.  
Rep. Green: You mentioned there would be a cost. How much would the alternate microphone setup cost?  
Chair Dr. Ackman: Stated that the cost would be approximately $2,000 and that the Committee should consider whether 
to reallocate funds or ask the City to cover the cost. 
Rep. Pitone: Thanked the Chair for addressing the issue and questioned why the District would be expected to cover 
the cost of equipment in a City facility. She also asked whether the City had provided a written  explanation 
Chair Dr. Ackman:  Stated that the City has not provided a written explanation and has only communicated its 
expectations regarding the cost. She noted that she had hoped Mayor Wilson would be present to address the matter.  
Council Davis: Stated that Mayor Wilson was attending other events and offered to discuss the matter with the Chair 
and Mayor Wilson outside of the meeting. He noted that he had only learned of the issue that afternoon and did not yet 
have all the details. He offered to work collaboratively toward a solution.
2 
 
  
Dr. Stellman: Asked how the microphone issue might affect City Council public comment and expressed support for 
working with the City to resolve the issue. 
Rep. Green: Noted that discussing staff by name during public comment is inconsistent with Committee policy and raises 
concerns under the collective bargaining agreement. She emphasized the importance of protecting staff and addressing 
potentially defamatory statements. 
Chair Dr. Ackman: Thanked Rep. Green for the clarification. 
Rep. Eldridge: Asked about the timeline for addressing the microphone issue and whether a quick fix was possible.  
Chair Dr. Ackman:  Stated that the alternate setup could likely be implemented quickly, while repairing the existing 
system would require significant work to the chamber floor. She will follow up with Council President Davis and Mayor 
Wilson, with the goal of resolving the issue by the next meeting. 
The Chair also noted that the September 21 School Committee meeting will be moved to September 28 due to Yom 
Kippur and reminded members about the MASC/MASS conference taking place November 4–6 in Danvers 
Rep. Pitone: Encouraged Committee members to attend the MASC/MASS conference for as much of the event as their 
schedules allow, noting that the conference has provided valuable opportunities for professional learning and networking 
with other School Committee members. 
Chair Dr. A ckman: Noted that the Superintendent and Assistant Superintendent will be presenting at this year’s 
conference with a consultant and an SPS parent who has volunteered their time to support the District. The session 
proposal was approved, and additional inf ormation will be shared as the conference approaches. The Chair then asked 
whether there were any additional community or calendar updates from Committee members and noted that the item 
could be revisited at the end of the meeting.   
II.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES 
● June 8, 2026 
● June 15, 2026 
● Special Meeting of the Whole August 10, 2026 
● Special Meeting of the Whole August 17, 2026 
●  
MOTION: there was a motion by Rep. Biton, seconded by Rep Green to approve the June 8, 2026, June 15, 
2026, Special Meeting of the Whole August 10, 2026 and Special Meeting of the Whole August 17, 2026 
regular School Committee meeting minutes. 
 
The motion was approved unanimously via roll call vote. 
 
III.  REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT 
 
A. District Report 
● School Readiness (DPW/IAM? 
 
Chair Dr. Ackman: Thanked everyone and acknowledged the first day of school, noting that it is unusual for the first 
School Committee meeting to coincide with the first day of school. She expressed appreciation for seeing photos of 
students returning to school and their excitement for the new school year. The Chair then moved to the Superintendent’s 
Report.  
Superintendent’s Notes: School Committee- Monday, August 31, 2026 
 
Superintendent Carmona: Welcomed everyone to the first day of school and presented his Superintendent’ s Report 
with a visual component. He highlighted the extensive preparation that takes place before the first day, including 
professional development, administrator preparation, and coordination across the District.  
He thanked educators and staff for their work in preparing for the school year and highlighted Convocation as an important 
opportunity for the District community to come together, recharge, and align around the priorities for the year.
3 
 
  
The Superintendent w elcomed students back and noted the excitement throughout the District’s schools. He also 
acknowledged the visit from the Commissioner and Secretary of Education and expressed appreciation for the recognition 
of Somerville’s work and diverse school communities. 
He thanked DPW and AM for their work preparing school buildings over the summer, noting that significant projects were 
completed within a limited timeframe while buildings were also being used for summer programming and professional 
development. 
The Superintendent then discussed the District’s instructional priorities, emphasizing that the focus this year is on 
strengthening and building upon existing initiatives rather than introducing new ones. He highlighted continued work 
around instructional implementation, building educator capacity, and increasing access to learning for students. He then 
turned the presentation over to Chief Strategy and Operations Officer Dr. Meekerley Sanon for a facilities update 
Dr. Sanon: First, on behalf of the Superintendent’s Office and the entire Somerville Public Schools community, I want to 
thank the Mayor, DPW, and IAM for all of their work preparing our schools for the start of the school year. They have 
heard a lot from us, including from me this morning, as we worked to make sure the schools were ready to open. We do 
not want to minimize the amount of work that goes into getting our schools ready. 
The report included in the packet was prepared by Eric Wiseman, who spent a great deal of time documenting the work 
completed over the summer. One thing that is mentioned briefly in the report is the short turnaround between the end 
of summer programming and the start of the school year. 
I am proud to share that several significant projects were completed over the summer, inclu ding upgrades to the 
Argenziano School kitchen. Accessibility concerns at Winter Hill were also addressed, although there are a few remaining 
items that we continue to work on. In addition, Phase One of the Kennedy School playground project has been completed. 
We are also closely monitoring several larger facilities projects to ensure that they do not interrupt school operations. In 
particular, at the West Somerville School, there is currently scaffolding in place, and we have spent a great deal of time 
making sure that the area is safe for our students. IAM and DPW have been very responsive in providing updates and 
assuring us that students will continue to be able to use the outdoor play areas. 
We have also completed HVAC upgrades and continue to follow up on concerns related to HVAC throughout the district. 
At Argenziano, we are continuing to prepare the building to welcome new programming in the upcoming school year.  
Finally, two large boilers were delivered to the building without issue and are expected to be installed during the school 
year. 
Rep. Green: I think it would be helpful to have a way to break down the work that has been completed compared with 
the work that is still pending. It is very helpful to see all of the work that DPW has accomplished, and it is impressive 
how much they are able to complete each summer despite the various constraints. However, it would also be helpful to 
understand what still needs to be done so we have a clearer picture of where we stand. A memo outlining the completed, 
in-progress, and pending work would be very helpful going forward. 
Dr. Sanon: On it. It sounds like a table showing the status of each project completed, in progress, and pending.  
Rep Biton: I was at West Somerville this morning and had the opportunity to walk around with Danielle Barry to see the 
roof work and scaffolding. Everything looked clean, orderly, and safe. No work was taking place today due to the start of 
school operations. I was very impressed with how the project is being managed and want to  thank the City, DPW, and 
our school-side team for their coordination.  
Chair Dr. Ackman:  I want to acknowledge the excellent communication around the facilities work. We had been 
anticipating seeing cranes above the school the weekend before school started, and Director Richter proactively reached 
out to make sure we knew the equipment would be removed before students arrived. The communication throughout 
the process has been top-notch. 
Mayor Wilson: At this morning’s Cabinet meeting, we heard about the ch allenging process of moving the new boilers 
into Argenziano. The boilers, which weigh approximately two tons each, had to be carefully maneuvered into the building 
and through the elevators. There were some concerns about whether they would fit, but the difficult part is now complete.
4 
 
  
The boilers are in the building and ready to be connected. 
This is an important step because if the existing boiler at Argenziano were to fail, there would not be a suitable location 
for a temporary mobile boiler, which could potentially have required the building to be vacated. Getting the new boilers 
into the building is therefore a significant accomplishment. 
Dr. Stellman: This question may be addressed during the academic portion of the presentation, so I’m happy to wait if 
needed. A few slides ago, Dr. Carmona discussed the work being done to support teachers with high-quality instructional 
materials. I’m curious about what is different in the approach this year and what new strategies are being used. I’m 
happy to wait until the academic portion of the presentation or hear any comments from Dr. Boston Davis.  
Superintendent Carmona: Highlighted the District’s instructional and academic priorities for the school year, centered 
on the rallying call, “Every student learns in ev ery class, every day.” He emphasized student engagement, productive 
struggle, and ensuring teachers have the tools and support needed to create strong learning conditions.  
He discussed strengthening the District’s data cycles by having teachers and administrators regularly review student data, 
identify areas for improvement, and adjust instruction accordingly. He also highlighted continued work on inclusive 
practices and special education supports. 
The Superintendent noted positive trends in recent assessment data, particularly in mathematics, while acknowledging 
continued achievement gaps and areas requiring additional support. He outlined five areas of focus: professional 
development, data cycles, inclusive practices, continued implementation and monitoring of XBlock, and partnerships to 
strengthen instruction in the early grades. 
He emphasized the importance of consistent implementation, ongoing monitoring, and collaboration between central 
office and school-based leaders. 
Rep. Pitone: Expressed appreciation for the District’s focus on the priority, “Every student learns in every class, every 
day.” She emphasized the importance of ensuring that families feel confident that their children are support ed and that 
their learning is a priority. She noted that the message reflects the commitment of families and educators across the 
District. 
Dr. Stellman:  Built on Rep. Pitone’s comments and highlighted the importance of focusing on day -to-day student 
behaviors and understanding individual students within the learning context. She asked what new or different approaches 
are being used to support educators as they implement new instructional practices in math, English, and other academic 
areas. 
Superintendent Carmona: Explained that the District is focused on identifying effective practices already taking place 
and replicating them across schools rather than reinventing existing approaches. He noted that the District has strong 
educators and practices in every building, but outcomes can vary between classrooms. He emphasized building more 
consistent and reliable systems through data monitoring, inquiry cycles, professional support, and partnerships. The goal 
is to better understand what is working, identify area s where students need additional support, and use data to make 
more precise instructional decisions. 
Dr. Boston Davis: Explained that the District is focusing on deepening existing practices rather than introducing new 
initiatives. Through the Barr Foundation grant, the District is investing in school leadership through coaching and training 
for principal supervisors, continued coaching for principals through Lynch Leadership Academy, and instructional rounds 
supported by an outside facilitator. 
She also highlighted the District’s new instructional coach model, with coaches supporting instruction in each school, as 
well as continued professional development focused on inclusive practices. Dr. Jenna Rufo will continue supporting 
administrators and district-wide professional development based on findings from the special education and intervention 
services review. 
Dr. Boston Davis emphasized that the goal is to strengthen implementation, improve consistency, and better support 
educators in meeting the needs of all students. 
Dr. Stellman: Praised the District’s approach to instructional leadership and expressed pride  in the work being done to
5 
 
  
support educators and administrators. 
Chair Dr. Ackman: Shared that the Superintendent reported to the Commissioner of Education that the District is nearly 
fully staffed, aside from a few remaining positions. She attributed this  in part to the District’s investment in and 
commitment to educators and recognized the Superintendent, Assistant Superintendent, and union for their work on the 
educators’ contract. 
Rep. Green: Commended the District’s focus on strengthening implementation rather than introducing unnecessary new 
initiatives. She highlighted the change in how building leaders are supervised, noting that distributing supervisory 
responsibilities should provide more consistent support and make it easier to implement instructional priorities across the 
District. 
Rep. Eldridge: Expressed enthusiasm for Focus Area 2 and the District’s efforts to strengthen a culture of data and 
support student success. She asked whether the K –3 focus on DIBELS could be expanded to K –2, emphasizin g the 
importance of early literacy intervention before students transition from learning to read to reading to learn.  
Dr. Boston Davis: Agreed with the importance of earlier intervention and noted that the District is partnering with Ignite 
Reading and Spr ingboard through early literacy initiatives, with a particular focus on first grade. She shared that the 
District is intentionally narrowing its focus and will revisit how the K–3 goal is reflected in its planning and initiatives. 
Superintendent Carmona: Shared his enthusiasm for the District’s partnership with Ignite Reading and its “First Grade 
Promise,” noting that achieving strong reading outcomes by the end of first grade could significantly impact student 
trajectories. He explained that the District w ill pilot the program in select schools while building capacity. He also 
highlighted positive teacher feedback on the new Foundations materials and noted progress across multiple areas of 
instruction. 
Dr. Boston Davis:  Added that the District is implementi ng high -quality instructional materials in K –2, including 
Foundations for structured literacy and Wit & Wisdom for reading comprehension and content. She noted that these 
initiatives align with the District’s focus on early literacy in K–2. 
Rep. Eldridge: Requested regular updates on the progress of first -grade students as the new literacy initiatives are 
implemented, including opportunities to monitor outcomes and make adjustments. She expressed enthusiasm for learning 
more about the impact on students. 
Rep. Lippens: Commended the presentation and the District’s focus on inclusive practices and high -quality curriculum. 
She noted the importance of maintaining and investing in strong instructional materials rather than introducing new 
initiatives each year. S he also asked about the systems and supports in place to ensure principals have the capacity to 
fully engage in the leadership development opportunities supported by the Barr Foundation grant.  
Superintendent Carmona: Explained that the District’s existing support systems including social workers, counselors, 
deans, restorative justice practices, and student services help principals focus more on instructional leadership. He noted 
that the District is continuing to strengthen these systems, integrate profess ional learning through TNTP and Lynch 
Leadership Academy, and use data to evaluate the effectiveness of its supports. He also emphasized that narrowing his 
direct supervision group will allow him to provide more focused support to building leaders while co ntinuing to examine 
schedules, support cycles, staff roles, and ways to distribute responsibilities effectively.  
Rep. Lippens: Summarized that the Superintendent is continuing to monitor and adjust the District’s systems based on 
data and asked if she understood correctly that he will be working with a smaller group of building leaders. Superintendent 
Carmona confirmed. 
Rep. Eldridge: Asked how Open Architects will support the District’s broader systems and data work and whether parents 
may have opportunities to access relevant data and information. 
Dr. Boston Davis: Explained that Open Architects will play a central role in strengthening the District’s data systems by 
helping teams focus on analyzing and responding to data rather than gathering it. She note d plans to use the platform 
with principals to guide inquiry and support data-informed leadership decisions, with Sam Eligene and Dr. Sanon playing 
key roles. She also shared that the District is exploring ways to expand the Strategic Plan family dashboard , including 
potentially providing families with access to DIBELS data for younger students. She welcomed ideas for making the use
6 
 
  
of data more transparent, collaborative, and accessible to families.  
Superintendent Carmona: Explained that Open Architects o ffers tools for families and teachers, and the District will 
explore the infrastructure, cost, and community education needed to make data more accessible. He emphasized the 
District’s commitment to transparency and serving the community effectively. He also recognized teachers for their work 
implementing new instructional programs across multiple content areas, noting that effective implementation takes time 
and that the District’s focus should be on building and replicating successful practices rather than continually introducing 
new initiatives.   
 
 B. Personal Report

Dr Carmona shared the personnel report and announced retirements

IV. REPORTS FROM SUBCOMMITTEES 
A. School Committee Meeting for the Educational Programs and Instruction Subcommittee:  
May 29, 2026 (Member Pitone) Tabled  
 
MOTION: There was a motion by Rep  Biton seconded by Rep Green to approve the following Subcommittee meeting 
Finance and Facilities from June 17th, Rules Management from June 15th, Rules  Management from July 9th, and Rules  
Management from August 20th  
The motion was approved unanimously via roll call vote. 
B. School Committee Meeting for the Finance and Facilities Subcommittee Meeting: J une 17, 2026 
(Member Green) 
June 17th, Finance Sub-committee 
In Attendance, A. Green, L. Biton, and E. Stellman. Also in attendance was CFO Beretta. There were also 2 people in 
the audience. The meeting was called to order at 7:01. 
First on the agenda was the FY26 year-to-date budget and projections. As of June 12, the district had invested 90% of 
the $19,116,847 non-personnel budget, with 21 of 32 departments at 90% or higher invested, ahead of last year's pace 
of 17 of 32 at the same point. Nine departments were running over budget, while several others remained under 65% 
invested. Remaining dollars are earmarked for reading and math curriculum, technology, and classroom furniture 
upgrades at West and East Somerville, with the district projected to end the year with a small balance split between the 
Special Ed Stabilization fund and capital projects. On the salary side, the Committee reviewed a budget of $94,861,856 
against $82,501,160 invested, with a projected year-end balance of $541,520 (0.6% of the salary budget), despite 
absorbing unbudgeted staffing needs, extraordinary substitute costs, and new CBA expenses.  
The Committee then reviewed the May investment roll, totaling $1,737,997.60 across strategic priorities including 
Wellness & Joy, Academic Excellence, and Equity & Access, with investments ranging from AV systems at two schools 
to mental health support vendors to instrument rentals for El Sistema. A motion to approve the May investment roll was 
moved by L. Biton and seconded by E. Stellman, which passed unanimously. 
The Committee then reviewed the FY27 Budget Book, which compiles all budget presentation materials into one 
document. The book is now translation-ready in Spanish and Portuguese, with a detailed appendix of financial reports 
for transparency. Staff noted plans for earlier publication and a more accessible presentation next year.  
Finally, the Committee reviewed its FY27 goals. Of the three set for the year, the district did not achieve 100% of non -
personnel budgets at 90% invested. The other two, improving the precision of the budgeting process and producing 
the Budget Book, were both achieved. The floor was then opened for discussion on how to improve the Finance
8 
 
  
SubCommittee for FY27. 
With no further business, the meeting adjourned at 7:47 pm. The Committee's next meeting is scheduled for 
September, the first Finance Sub-Committee of FY27. 
 
C. School Committee Meeting for the Rules Management Subcommittee Meeting: June 15, 2026  
(Member Biton) 
  Report to School Committee on the 
 Rules Management Subcommittee Meeting for June 15, 2026 
To: Somerville School Committee 
From: Leiran Biton, Chair of the Rules Management Subcommittee 
  
The School Committee (SC) Rules Management Subcommittee met on June 15, 2026, at the Somer ville City Council 
Chambers. 
  
Attending: 
·         School Committee members: Leiran Biton, chair; Dr. Emma Stellman, vice chair; Michele Lippens.  
There was one member in the audience. 
The chair called the subcommittee meeting to order and established quorum with Mr. Biton, Dr. Stellman, and Ms. 
Lippens present at 5:39 p.m. 
1)      Approval of the report from the May 18, 2026 Meeting 
Approved. 
2)      MASC Policy Manual Review (Section J) 
The subcommittee continued its comprehensive review of Section J. 
·         Policy JII - Student Complaints and Grievances: The subcommittee reviewed updated 
language regarding mechanisms for students to appeal disciplinary decisions. Dr. Stellman and Ms . 
Lippens questioned the specific “appropriate channels” for these grievances and whether they are 
clearly defined for parents and students in school handbooks. Mr. Biton suggested that these 
details are often procedural handbook language rather than broad policy. The subcommittee tabled 
this policy to seek administrative input on whether the current grievance process is functioning 
effectively. 
·         Policy JJ - Co-Curricular and Extracurricular Activities: Dr. Stellman expressed concern 
regarding dated language in the Somerville version, specifically the phrase “developing wholesome 
attitudes”. The subcommittee agreed the policy requires a significant update to align with 2026 
standards. Dr. Stellman will take the lead on overhauling this policy for future review. 
·         Policy JJ-E - Co-Curricular and Extra-Curricular Activities (Exhibit): The subcommittee 
identified a need to modernize gender-related language, such as changing “both sexes” to 
“students of all genders”. Dr. Stellman noted historical misalignments in resources provided for 
different athletic programs. The group also discussed the importance of codifying protections for 
transgender and non-binary athletes. Mr. Biton will relay a request for feedback on this policy to 
Athletic Director Vieira and the Director of Equity through the Superintendent.
9 
 
  
·         Policy JJA - Student Organizations: Member Lippens criticized the current criteria for student 
organizations (i.e., “contributing to student self-esteem and performance”) as potentially limiting 
and difficult to measure. Dr. Stellman noted the high school version already aligns organizations 
with the school mission. The subcommittee tabled this item to search for existing, vetted language 
in current handbooks and to seek direct input from student representatives. 
·         Policy JJE - Student Fundraising Activities: The subcommittee reviewed the 2025 MASC 
model policy. The committee agreed on a change to the text from recognizing that families have 
different resources to “different priorities and resources.” The group decided to consult student 
representatives for their insight into modern, peer-to-peer fundraising challenges before finalizing. 
Following a discussion on how to best reach student representatives, the chair committed to coordinate with staff to 
establish a process for adding subcommittee agenda items to student council meetings. This will allow the 
subcommittee to receive formal student feedback on policies like JJA and JJE starting in the fall.  
The subcommittee plans to hold two virtual meetings over the summer in July and August to continue t he manual 
review. 
The chair adjourned the meeting at 6:28 p.m. 
  
D. School Committee Meeting for the Rules Management Subcommittee Meeting: July 9, 2026 (Member 
Biton) 
Report to School Committee on the 
Rules Management Subcommittee Meeting for July 9, 2026 
 
To: Somerville School Committee 
From: Leiran Biton, Chair of the Rules Management Subcommittee 
  
The School Committee (SC) Rules Management Subcommittee met on July 9, 2026, virtually on Zoom.  
  
Attending: 
·         School Committee: Leiran Biton, chair; Dr. Emma Stellman, vice chair; Michele Lippens.  
·         SPS: Darryl Nash, SPS Communications Director. 
·         Alicia Mallon, MASC Field Director 
There were two members in the audience. 
The chair called the subcommittee meeting to order and established quorum with Mr. Biton, Dr. Stellman, and Ms. Lippens 
present at 5:36 p.m. 
1)      Approval of the report from the June 15, 2026 Meeting 
Approved unanimously

Dr. Stellman, the lead for this item, provided an update on her research regarding the prevalence of harmful

Ms. Mallon shared a completely rewritten version of Policy JKAA, updated to encompass a comprehensive 
“Time-out, Seclusion, and Physical Restraint of Students” policy based directly on recent Department of 
Elementary and Secondary Education (DESE) guidance. Dr. Stellman noted that the checklist -oriented, 
operational format of the policy is highly useful for educators making rapid decisions. Ms. Mallon noted that 
although procedures are typically kept separate from high-level policy, MASC legal counsel included these 
details because DESE indicated districts must have them.
